segments: "The key to understanding Nix code is knowing where each variable comes from."
This is the most common way to define local variables.
Rule: let bindings are visible within every binding's value and the expression after in, so bindings can refer to one another. They do not leak outside the expression.
Use inherit when you want to assign a variable to an attribute with the same name.
This is extremely common in flake.nix and module configurations.
with set; body adds an attribute-lookup scope for body. Existing lexical bindings take precedence; it does not turn the attributes into ordinary let bindings.
Risk: variable-name collisions become easy to introduce and difficult to debug, since it may be unclear whether a variable comes from pkgs or the global scope.
Recommendation: using it inside lists [ ... ] is fine, but use it sparingly in large configuration blocks.
The top level of a Nix file is often an anonymous function:
... (Ellipsis): indicates that the function accepts additional arguments it does not currently need, preventing errors from an argument mismatch.
Destructuring: specify the parameter names you need directly inside the braces.
